The question this page answers

What do remittances and other money flows tell us about households’ connection to the financial system?

Remittances: each figure depends on its source, concept and edition

Report an error

For the 2024 reference year, the 2024 annual report of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) gave remittances of US$6,245 million, and its 2025 annual report restated the same year at US$3,422.16 million: a revision of the same year, not a fall. Macro inflows, corridor prices and household receipt channels answer different questions, so this resource keeps these evidence records separate and makes revisions visible.

Explore questionsOpen evidence
What this does not establish

What remittance evidence does not establish

A macro remittance series does not equal informal hawala volume or household distribution. A source revision is not an economic fall. Similar paths after indexing to 2021 = 100 do not prove that two raw series have the same scope or reveal a conversion factor. Corridor prices are not a national cost average. A change in an external stock is not automatically a transaction, and BPM7, the updated international standard for balance-of-payments statistics, does not retroactively rewrite Yemen’s historical series without an explicit conversion.

What we still do not know

What remains unresolved

The exact public crosswalk between key external-sector series of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) and the IMF remains open. For 2024, CBY-Aden’s 2025 annual report gives remittances of US$3,422.16 million, while the IMF’s 2025 Article IV staff report gives US$1,861.7 million on the IMF’s analytical scope for areas under the internationally recognized government. Over 2021–2024 the two series differ by a roughly constant ratio of 1.838 and their indexed growth paths almost coincide; what that ratio represents is not established, so neither level can be converted into the other. Current household receipt and channel behaviour, and the scale of informal channels, are also not established by the macro and corridor evidence.

03Analysis

Reported history, estimates and projections are different kinds of evidence

The IMF staff report gives 2018–2024 as reported history based on staff calculations; a later supplement to the same consultation gives 2025 as an estimate and 2026–2030 as projections. The series is kept apart where the source document changes: reported history is never extended through the forecast as if all years had the same status. A forecast revision is not an observed economic change, and the macro series is not a measure of informal hawala volume.

Another view of the evidence
04Analysis

The same reference year can change when the source publishes a new edition

For the 2024 reference year, the 2024 annual report of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) gave US$6,245 million, while its 2025 annual report restated 2024 at US$3,422.16 million. That is a same-year source revision, not a year-on-year fall. The later path also shows unusually similar growth rates across overlapping years; that invites method scrutiny but does not establish smoothing or interpolation.

05Evidence

A reconstruction effort is documented; the exact crosswalk is not

IMF documents a 2024–2025 external-sector statistics reconstruction effort with the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) and a July 2025 mission that produced balance-of-payments (BOP) and international investment position (IIP) statistics for 2014–2024. It also documents a demographic-behavioural personal-transfer model where informal-channel data were limited. This establishes method context, not the exact formula behind every value in CBY-Aden annual reports. The public CBY-Aden and IMF components tested here do not support a single conversion factor for all series.

06Analysis

Cost depends on corridor and transfer size

In 2025 Q3, quoted averages for Saudi Arabia–Yemen were 2.70% at US$200 and 1.26% at US$500. For UAE–Yemen they were 7.53% and 5.62%. The difference shows why transfer size and corridor must stay visible. These quotes do not cover every provider or informal channel and must not be collapsed into one national remittance-cost rate.

System context

Household behaviour is a different evidence layer

The 2014 weighted World Bank profile reported 18.3% of adults receiving domestic remittances. Among recipients—not all adults—31.1% reported a money-transfer operator, 2.0% a financial institution and 0.0% mobile phone. Those historical channel shares cannot be converted into current monetary-flow shares, but they provide a bounded people-side context for how remittances were received in that survey wave (round).

Analysis

Before ranking external flows, inspect the balancing residual

In the 2025 annual report of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), net errors and omissions exceed the published remittance line in every year from 2021 through 2025; in 2025 the residual is about US$7.117 billion against US$3.614 billion in remittances, or 1.97 times the remittance line. Net errors and omissions are a balancing residual, not an observed flow and not a hidden-remittance estimate.

Same year, different number
Successive annual reports of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden give very different remittance values for 2024. A revision of this size is a measurement event to be explained before it can be read as an economic story.

What measurement would change the decision?

Measurement priorityP0 · People
A current people-side inclusion baseline
The Global Findex 2025 edition contains 2024 observations for many economies, but Yemen's latest representative account-ownership observation remains 11.9% of adults aged 15 and over in the areas surveyed, for 2022 (from the Yemen Findex 2021 study fielded in 2022–2023). Major payment-system and reform changes are more recent. The latest published people-level values for receiving domestic remittances, and through which channels, are from 2014; the 2021-wave microdata contain these questions, but weighted estimates have not yet been produced.
Evidence needed: New representative Yemen demand-side survey or equivalent approved microdata with weights and clear coverage, including remittance receipt, channel and frequency.
Decision it would strengthen: A current population measure would allow change since the previous wave to be assessed without projecting reform results onto the population.

When was it measured or observed?Reported history 2018–2024 (staff calculations); estimate 2025; projection 2026–2030
IMF remittance series: reported history, estimates and projections kept separate
The history in the IMF 2025 Article IV staff report gives a higher value for remittance inflows in 2024 than in 2018 (both values from the same document); the 2025 estimate and the 2026–2030 projections come from a later supplement and are estimates and projections, not reported values. The IMF series covers the IMF's analytical scope for areas under the internationally recognized government, so its level is not a whole-of-Yemen figure and is not comparable in level with the annual-report values of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden).
Who or what does it apply to? External-sector macro concept, on the IMF's analytical scope for areas under the internationally recognized government
Open evidence record
When was it measured or observed?Reference years 2020–2025 in the 2022–2025 annual reports; IMF method work 2024–2025
Same reference year, different published value
Annual reports of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) publish materially different remittance values for the same reference year. For 2024, the 2024 annual report gave USD 6,245 million, while the 2025 annual report restated 2024 at USD 3,422.16 million. This is a same-year restatement, not evidence of economic movement between years. The same holds further back. For reference year 2021, the 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 editions of the annual report give USD 4,043, 5,400.0, 5,625 and 2,900.22 million; for reference year 2022, they give USD 4,454, 6,000, 6,000 and 3,066.58 million. These are successive editions' values for one year, not a series over time.
Who or what does it apply to? The remittance series published in the balance of payments of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden); its exact territorial and conceptual mapping to the IMF reconstruction for areas under the internationally recognized government remains open
Open evidence record
When was it measured or observed?Overlapping reference years 2021–2024 in the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) Annual Report 2025 and the IMF 2025 Article IV consultation
The published CBY and IMF balance-of-payments components tested do not support a single conversion factor
Across the public balance-of-payments components tested for 2021–2024, from the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) Annual Report 2025 and from the IMF series for areas under the internationally recognized government, the evidence does not support a single conversion factor. The remittance ratio is almost constant, but the ratios for imports, grants, the current account and net errors and omissions differ materially, and the IMF documents component-specific sources and transformations. This does not rule out component-specific bridges or a future official crosswalk.
Who or what does it apply to? Only the public CBY and IMF balance-of-payments components actually tested; each component retains its source definition, geography and transformation.

Before ranking flows, look at the balancing residual
In the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) Annual Report 2025, net errors and omissions are larger than the published remittance line in every year from 2021 to 2025. In 2025 the residual is USD 7.117 billion against USD 3.614 billion for remittances, 1.97 times the remittance line. Net errors and omissions is a balancing residual, not an observed flow or an estimate of hidden remittances.
Who or what does it apply to? The balance of payments as each source defines it
